_comment: Scoped policy for the `auth-service` MEDIA account (uploads AND playback).
Why this account exists at all:
- `wideo11-auth-avatars` (auth-avatars.json) is scoped to `avatars` and
`covers`. That is correct for profile images and channel covers, and it
is also why `POST /media/initiate` was minting presigned PUT URLs to the
`video` bucket with an account that had NO rights there. Every video
upload failed with `AccessDenied` - not a code bug, a provisioning one.
- `wideo11-transcode-video` (transcode-video.json) is scoped to `video`
with READ and WRITE. auth-service cannot use it: the compose file
documents exactly why - 'granting it `video` would put every user's
source media behind the service that mints profile-image URLs.'
So the media lifecycle gets its own account, scoped to the ONE bucket it
needs:
- `s3:PutObject` on `video/*`   - mints a presigned PUT the browser uses
- `s3:GetObject` on `video/*`   - mints the presigned GET for playback and
for the poster, because a signed URL is
presented to MinIO AS this account and
MinIO checks ITS rights
- NOTHING at the bucket level   - it cannot LIST, so it cannot enumerate
any other user's filenames
- NOTHING on `avatars` / `covers` / `thumbnails`
No `s3:DeleteBucket`, no `s3:PutBucketPolicy`, no admin actions, no
`s3:ListBucket` on `video` itself. It can fetch and write objects inside one
bucket and cannot see any other.
A leaked key therefore reads and writes `video/*` and nothing else - and
cannot enumerate the bucket to learn what is in it. That is the blast
radius, and it is the smallest one that supports upload plus playback.
Ownership is NOT enforced here and cannot be: the media rows are in Postgres,
and MinIO has no idea who owns an object. The service layer checks that the
caller owns the asset before it will sign anything - see
`MediaService.SignedObjectURL`.
PutObject on the objects, and NOTHING at the bucket level.
That omission is deliberate, and it was caught by the assertion in
init-storage.sh: an earlier draft carried `s3:ListBucket` on
`arn:aws:s3:::video`, so `mc ls uploader/video` SUCCEEDED. That is a
leak - it enumerates every object key in the bucket, which is every
user's source filename. minio-init now dies on that, which is the whole
point of asserting behaviour instead of reading the policy back.
Signing needs no bucket-level action either: minio-go computes the
request signature locally, and the region is set explicitly on the
client rather than discovered with a GetBucketLocation round trip.
GetObject IS here, and it was not in the first draft. Without it the
account could mint an upload URL and then be unable to mint the PLAYBACK
URL for the same object - a signed GET is presented to MinIO as this
account, so MinIO checks ITS permissions and refuses. The result was a
finished upload whose poster and playlist both returned AccessDenied,
which is why the bucket being private was showing up as a bug rather
than as the intended security posture.
Read is still scoped to `video/*` and to nothing else, and the bucket
itself stays unlistable - so this account can fetch ONE object it was
asked about and cannot enumerate the names of the others.
